(p-148)Surah al-Ghashiyah (The Overwhelming)

Makkan, and its verses number twenty-six.

﴿Has the news of the Overwhelming Event come to you?﴾ It has been said: "hal" here means "qad" (indeed), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time...﴾ (76:1). Qutrub said: that is, "Indeed the news of the Overwhelming Event has come to you, O Muhammad." But this is not the case. Rather, it is an interrogative used to express wonder at what it contains, to arouse eagerness to hear it, and to indicate that it is one of the wondrous reports which the narrators ought to pass on to one another, and which the memorizers ought to compete in receiving, from every person present and every person of the desert.

Al-ghashiyah (the Overwhelming) is the severe calamity that covers people with its hardships and surrounds them with its terrors, and it is the Resurrection, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day the punishment will overwhelm them﴾ ... etc. It has also been said that it is the Fire, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Fire will cover their faces﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and above them will be coverings (ghawashin)﴾. The first is the correct view, for what will be related of its news is not restricted to the Fire and its people; rather, it also speaks of the conditions of the people of Paradise.

And His saying, ﴿Faces, that Day, humbled﴾ up to His saying, ﴿scattered﴾, is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) that came as an answer to a question arising from a rhetorical interrogation meant to arouse interest (*istifham tashwiqi*). It is as if it were said: "Concerning it, upon him be prayer and peace, the news of it has not come to me, so what is it?" Then it was said: ﴿Faces, that Day﴾, i.e., on the day when it envelops, [they are] humbled. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The news of it had not come to him, upon him be prayer and peace, so he informed him about it, and said: ﴿Faces...﴾ etc. So *wujūh* (faces) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and there is no harm in its being indefinite, because it stands in the position of classification (*tanwī'*). *Khāshi'a* (humbled) is its predicate (*khabar*).

Its saying, ﴿Toiling, weary﴾, are two further predicates of "faces" (wujuh), since what is meant by them is their owners: that is, they labour at arduous tasks in which they are exhausted, namely dragging chains and shackles, wading into the Fire the way camels wade into mud, and climbing up and down the hills and valleys of the Fire. It has also been said: they laboured in the world at evil deeds and took pleasure in them, so they are on that Day in weariness from them. And it has been said: they toiled and grew weary at deeds that will avail them nothing in the Hereafter.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 88, verse 4:

And His saying, Most High: ﴿They will enter﴾ i.e., they will enter (tadkhulu).

﴿A scorching fire﴾ i.e., intensely hot, is a second predicate (khabar) for "faces (wujuh)." It has been said that this predicate and what precedes it are attributes (sifat) of "faces," and it has already been mentioned more than once that the attribute ought to be known (ma'lumah) to the hearer as belonging to the described noun (al-intisab ila al-mawsuf 'inda al-sami' qabla ja'liha sifatan lahu) before it is made an attribute of it. There is no doubt that the burning of the fire, and what precedes it of humility (khushu'), labor, and fatigue (nasab), are matters equal in their relation to the faces, both in being known and in being unknown. So making some of them a heading for the subject, a restriction already settled and not intended for informing, while making others the basis of the informing, is pure arbitrariness. It is also permissible that this and what follows it of the two sentences be a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the details of their conditions.
﴿They will be given drink from a spring, boiling hot﴾, meaning: extremely hot. As in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and between it and boiling hot water﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 88, verse 6:

﴿There is no food for them except from ḍarī'⟩ — an explanation of their food following the explanation of their drink. Ḍarī' (a dry, withered plant) is the dried-out state of al-shibriq, which is a thorny plant that camels graze while it is fresh; once it dries out, they shun it, and it is a deadly poison. It has been said that it is a fiery tree resembling ḍarī'. Ibn Kaysan said: it is a food over which they humble themselves, become abased, and beseech God Most High, seeking deliverance from it, and so it was named thus. This is the food of some of the people of the Fire, while zaqqum and ghislin are for others.

﴿It will neither nourish nor satisfy hunger.﴾ That is, it is not in its nature to fatten or to satisfy, as is the nature of the food of this world. Rather, it is something they are compelled to eat without it removing their need. Yet this is not on the basis that they have any readiness for satiety and fattening, but it gives them nothing of either. Rather, it is on the basis that there is neither readiness on their part nor benefit from their food. The verification of this is that their hunger and thirst are not of the kind known in this world: a condition that befalls a human when nature calls for a replacement for what the body loses, stirring him toward food and drink, so that he takes pleasure in them while eating and drinking, is satisfied by them without seeking anything else once they settle in the stomach, and gains strength and fattening from them when they are digested. Rather, their hunger is an expression of a fire blazing in their bowels that demands the introduction of something dense to fill it and drive out the flame within it. As for their having any longing for some food, or taking pleasure in it when eating, or being satisfied by it without seeking anything else, or gaining strength from it, that is far-fetched. Likewise, their thirst is an expression of their compulsion, when eating the ḍarī' (a thorny plant), and the burning of it in their bellies, toward something liquid and cold that extinguishes it, without their taking pleasure in drinking it or gaining any strength from it in general. This is what is meant by the report that He, exalted is He, will impose hunger upon them to the point of compelling them to eat the ḍarī'; then, when they have eaten it, He will impose thirst upon them, compelling them to drink ḥamīm (boiling water), which will scorch their faces and cut their intestines.

The indefiniteness of ﴿جُوعٍ﴾ (jū‘in, "hunger") is for belittlement, meaning: it does not satisfy any hunger whatsoever. The negation of satisfaction is placed after the negation of fattening for the sake of observing the al-fawāṣil (verse-endings) and in order to lead to an explicit negation of both matters. For if it had been placed first, there would have been no need to mention the negation of fattening, since the negation of satisfying hunger necessarily implies the negation of fattening; the reverse is not the case. For this reason, "lā" (no) is repeated to emphasize the negation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 88, verse 8:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Faces that Day will be joyful﴾. It is a beginning in narrating the account of the people of Paradise, and the mention of the condition of the people of the Fire is placed first, because it is more fitting for the awe-inspiring nature of the Overwhelming (al-Ghashiyah) and the magnification of its account; and because relating the good condition of the people of Paradise after relating the evil condition of the people of the Fire adds to what is related both goodness and delight. The discussion regarding the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this sentence is like that which has passed concerning its counterpart. It is not joined to it by a conjunction (lam tu'taf) to signify the complete contrast between their two meanings. The meaning of "joyful" (na'imah) is: possessing radiance and beauty, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾, or "enjoying comfort" (mutana''imah).
Quranic verse (88:9): ﴿Pleased with its striving.﴾ That is: pleased with its labor which it performed in the world, since it has witnessed its fruit.

Translation of the commentary on 88:10:

﴿In a lofty garden﴾: elevated in station, or exalted in rank.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 88, verse 11:

﴿Thou shalt not hear﴾ i.e., you (addressed to the Prophet) or the faces (i.e., the faces are the subject).

﴿therein any idle talk﴾: idle talk (laghw), or a word that carries idle talk, or a soul that engages in idle talk. For the speech of the people of Paradise is entirely remembrances of God (adhkar) and wise sayings (hikam). It has also been read as "lā tusma'" in the passive voice, with the yā' and the tā', and with "lāghiyatan" in the nominative.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 88, verse 12:

﴿Therein is a flowing spring﴾. That is: there are many springs whose waters flow, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a soul will know﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 88, verse 13:

﴿Therein are raised couches﴾ (sururun marfu'ah), lofty in height or in dimension.

﴿And cups﴾ is the plural of kub (cup), which is a vessel with no handle.

﴿Set in place﴾, i.e., placed before them.

**Translation:**

﴿And cushions﴾: pillows, the plural of *namruqah*, pronounced with either a fatha or a damma.

﴿Arranged in rows﴾: some of them placed alongside others.

﴿Zarabiyyu﴾ (carpets): that is, costly spreads, the plural of zirbiyya.

﴿mabthuthatun﴾ (spread out): that is, laid out.

﴿Will they not then look at the camels, how they have been created?﴾ This is a resumptive statement (*istinaf*), brought to affirm what was detailed in the account of the Overwhelming Event (*al-Ghashiyah*), and what is built upon it of the Resurrection, about which they dispute. It is established by citing evidence they cannot deny. The *hamzah* is for rebuke and reproach, and the *fa'* is for coordination with an implied element that the context requires. The word "كَيْفَ" (*kayfa*, "how") is in the accusative, governed by what follows it, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿How do you disbelieve in God?﴾ (2:28). It is suspended from the verb of looking (*ta'liq*). The clause is in the place of the genitive, as a comprehensive apposition (*badal al-ishtimal*) of "the camels." The meaning is: Do they deny what has been mentioned of the Resurrection and its rulings, and regard its occurrence as improbable from the power of God, Mighty and Majestic? Then do they not look at the camels, which are before their eyes, which they use at all times, to see how they were created (*khuliqat*) as a wondrous creation, distinguished from the customary patterns of the creation of the rest of the kinds of animals in the magnitude of their bodies, the intensity of their strength, and the marvelous form suited to their being able to perform the arduous tasks that proceed from them, such as kneeling under heavy loads and dragging burdensome weights to distant regions. Consider also their endurance of hunger and thirst, to the extent that their thirst may reach ten days or more; their contentment with little; and their grazing on whatever is available of thorns, trees, and other things that most beasts can hardly graze. Consider also their submission, despite all this, to humans in movement and rest, in kneeling and rising, where a person uses them for these as he wills and leads them by their halter, every young and old one of them. (p-151)

And at the sky, which they see every moment by night and day,

how it has been raised, raised to a vast height, without pillar or support, to such an extent that understanding and perception cannot reach it.

﴿And at the mountains﴾ which they descend to in their regions and benefit from their waters and trees.

﴿How they have been raised﴾ raised firmly, so they are fixed, not inclining nor swaying.

And at the earth, how it has been spread out (﴿وَإلى الأرْضِ﴾ الَّتِي يَضْرِبُونَ فِيها ويَتَقَلَّبُونَ عَلَيْها)—the earth in which they travel and upon which they move about.

﴿كَيْفَ سُطِحَتْ﴾: spread out (سَطْحًا) with leveling, smoothing, making even, and firm establishment, in accordance with what the welfare of the affairs of the creatures upon it requires. It is also read as "سُطِّحَتْ" with shaddah (intensive form). The four verbs are read with the first person singular active form (the speaker being God), with the returning pronoun in the accusative omitted. The meaning: Will they not look with the look of reflection and consideration at the manner in which these created things were made, which bear witness to the truth of the resurrection and rising again, so that they may turn back from their denial and aversion, listen to your warning, and prepare for meeting Him through faith and obedience.

The fa' (the particle of consequence) in His exalted saying ﴿So remind﴾ indicates that the command to remind follows from what the preceding denial of reflection implies. That is: confine yourself to reminding, do not press them, and do not let it trouble you that they do not reflect or take heed. His exalted saying ﴿Indeed you are only a reminder﴾ gives the reason (ta'lil, causal explanation) for the command.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 88, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ is a confirmation of it (the preceding command to remind) and a verification of the meaning of warning. That is: you are not one who dominates them, compelling them to do what you desire, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾. It has been recited with the sin (ص/س: "bi-l-sin") according to the original form, and with ishmam (a faint sound of "z" mixed with the "s"). It has also been recited with a fathah on the ta' (لَسْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِمُسَيْطِرٍ). It is said that this is the dialect of the Banu Tamtam, for "sayṭara" among them is transitive, and from it is their saying: tusayṭiru (you dominate).

In the Almighty's words, ﴿Except for one who turns away and disbelieves﴾, the exception is disjunct (munqati'), meaning: but as for whoever among them turns away, then God Most High has the mastery and the subjugation.

ﷻ﴿So Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment﴾, which is the punishment of Jahannam (Hellfire). It has also been said: this is an exception that is connected (istithna' muttasil) to His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿so remind﴾; that is, "So remind, except the one whose hope of his faith you have cut off and who turned away, so he deserves the greatest punishment," and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad). What supports the first view is that it has been read as "ala" (ألا), as an alert (tanbih).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 88, verse 25:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾, is a justification (ta'lil) for His punishing them with the greatest punishment, meaning: indeed, to Us is their return by death and resurrection, not to anyone other than Us, neither independently nor in partnership. The pronoun in it and in what follows is made plural in consideration of the meaning of "man" (man), just as its singular form in what preceded is in consideration of its wording. It is also read "iyabahum" (إيابَهُمْ), as a fi'yal form, a verbal noun of fay'al from al-iyab (return), or a fi'al form from awaba, like fisar (فِسارٌ) for one who interprets (fassara). Then it was said "iyawaban," like diwan (دِيُوانٌ) in diwwan (دِوّانٌ); then the waw was changed to a ya', and the first ya' was assimilated into the second.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 88, verse 26:

﴿Then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning﴾ at the Gathering (al-mahshar), not upon anyone other than Us. And "thumma" (then) here indicates distance in rank, not in time, for the temporal sequence is between their return (iyab) and their reckoning, not between the fact that their return is to Him, exalted is He, and the fact that their reckoning is upon Him, exalted is He, since these are two continuous matters. In beginning the two clauses with inna (indeed), placing its predicate first, and conjoining the second to the first with the word "thumma," which conveys the great remoteness of the reckoning's rank in severity, there is an indication of the utmost wrath that necessitates the intensification of punishment, which is not hidden.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Ghashiyah, Allah will reckon with him a light reckoning."
